resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
resources.abstract: The problem of privacy-preserving data analysis has a long history spanning multiple disciplines. As electronic data about individuals becomes increasingly detailed, and as technology enables ever more powerful collection and curation of these data, the need increases for a robust, meaningful, and mathematically rigorous definition of privacy, together with a computationally rich class of algorithms that satisfy this definition. Differential Privacy is such a definition. After motivating and discussing the meaning of differential privacy, the preponderance of this monograph is devoted to fundamental techniques for achieving differential privacy, and application of these techniques in creative combinations, using the query-release problem as an ongoing example. A key point is that, by rethinking the computational goal, one can often obtain far better results than would be achieved by methodically replacing each step of a non-private computation with a differentially private implementation. Despite some astonishingly powerful computational results, there are still fundamental limitations — not just on what can be achieved with differential privacy but on what can be achieved with any method that protects against a complete breakdown in privacy. Virtually all the algorithms discussed herein maintain differential privacy against adversaries of arbitrary computational power. Certain algorithms are computationally intensive, others are efficient. Computational complexity for the adversary and the algorithm are both discussed. We then turn from fundamentals to applications other than queryrelease, discussing differentially private methods for mechanism design and machine learning. The vast majority of the literature on differentially private algorithms considers a single, static, database that is subject to many analyses. Differential privacy in other models, including distributed databases and computations on data streams is discussed. Finally, we note that this work is meant as a thorough introduction to the problems and techniques of differential privacy, but is not intended to be an exhaustive survey — there is by now a vast amount of work in differential privacy, and we can cover only a small portion of it.

resources.title: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis
Programming Differential Privacy
The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm
resources.abstract: The Census TopDown Algorithm (TDA) is a disclosure avoidance system using differential privacy for privacy-loss accounting.The algorithm ingests the final, edited version of the 2020 Census data and the final tabulation geographic definitions.The algorithm then creates noisy versions of key queries on the data, referred to as measurements, using zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy.Another key aspect of the TDA are invariants, statistics that the Census Bureau has determined, as matter of policy, to exclude from the privacyloss accounting.The TDA postprocesses the measurements together with the invariants to produce a Microdata Detail File (MDF) that contains one record for each person and one record for each housing unit enumerated in the 2020 Census.The MDF is passed to the 2020 Census tabulation system to produce the 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File.This article describes the mathematics and testing of the TDA for this purpose.

resources.title: RAPPOR
resources.abstract: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response, or RAPPOR, is a technology for crowdsourcing statistics from end-user client software, anonymously, with strong privacy guarantees. In short, RAPPORs allow the forest of client data to be studied, without permitting the possibility of looking at individual trees. By applying randomized response in a novel manner, RAPPOR provides the mechanisms for such collection as well as for efficient, high-utility analysis of the collected data. In particular, RAPPOR permits statistics to be collected on the population of client-side strings with strong privacy guarantees for each client, and without linkability of their reports. This paper describes and motivates RAPPOR, details its differential-privacy and utility guarantees, discusses its practical deployment and properties in the face of different attack models, and, finally, gives results of its application to both synthetic and real-world data.

sample_claims.text: The census data analysis results remain statistically indistinguishable whether any single household's data is included or excluded
The medical research system's published statistics provide quantified privacy guarantees that bound the maximum disclosure risk for any individual patient
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters
The system's privacy protection level is mathematically bounded and remains effective even under repeated queries within the allocated budget

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

resources.title: Regression Quantiles
Quantile regression
Using quantile regression to extend an existing wind power forecasting system with probabilistic forecasts
resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

techniques.name: Conformal Prediction
techniques.description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

example_use_cases.description: A medicinal chemistry team screening compounds in silico builds prediction sets of the protein targets each compound may be active against, at 95% coverage. Compounds with a single-target set go to lab testing for that target, and those with several targets go to a wider panel, so costly experiments follow how uncertain the model is.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories at the stated coverage level, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

A university predicts whether first-year students will complete their degree and offers early support when the 90% prediction set includes 'withdraws'. To keep that 90% true for every group, not only on average, the data team calibrates the sets separately within each demographic group, then checks coverage and average set size per group on held-out students. A group with too few calibration cases is reported as not covered by the guarantee.

limitations.description: Sets can be wide enough to be useless. A multi-class set holding most classes, or an interval spanning the plausible range, meets the coverage target but tells the decision-maker little, and sets containing opposing outcomes make decisions hard. Width depends on the model's quality and the scoring rule chosen, and the guarantee says nothing about it.

Needs labelled calibration data kept apart from training. On small datasets that means less data to train on, or a coarse and unstable coverage level, and variants that avoid a separate calibration set need several model fits.

The guarantee assumes calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. Drift, a changed population or strongly time-ordered data break it, and coverage then falls below target with no warning. In Shafer and Vovk's example, a nominal 5% error rate rose to 8% on a systematically different test set.

Coverage is guaranteed on average over all cases, not for each individual or subgroup, so a model can reach 95% overall while covering a minority group far less often. Mondrian calibration fixes this only for predefined, non-overlapping groups. It needs each new case's group at prediction time and is unstable when a group has few calibration cases (MAPIE's tutorial gives under 200 as an example).

Cost depends on the variant. Split conformal prediction adds little beyond scoring a held-out set, but full conformal prediction re-evaluates every candidate outcome and cross-conformal variants refit the model several times, which can be prohibitive for large models or real-time use.

resources.title: MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator
MAPIE
resources.abstract: A scikit-learn-compatible library for estimating prediction intervals and controlling risks, based on conformal predictions.

resources.title: A tutorial on conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Conformal prediction uses past experience to determine precise levels of confidence in new predictions. Given an error probability $ε$, together with a method that makes a prediction $\hat{y}$ of a label $y$, it produces a set of labels, typically containing $\hat{y}$, that also contains $y$ with probability $1-ε$. Conformal prediction can be applied to any method for producing $\hat{y}$: a nearest-neighbor method, a support-vector machine, ridge regression, etc.   Conformal prediction is designed for an on-line setting in which labels are predicted successively, each one being revealed before the next is predicted. The most novel and valuable feature of conformal prediction is that if the successive examples are sampled independently from the same distribution, then the successive predictions will be right $1-ε$ of the time, even though they are based on an accumulating dataset rather than on independent datasets.   In addition to the model under which successive examples are sampled independently, other on-line compression models can also use conformal prediction. The widely used Gaussian linear model is one of these.   This tutorial presents a self-contained account of the theory of conformal prediction and works through several numerical examples. A more comprehensive treatment of the topic is provided in "Algorithmic Learning in a Random World", by Vladimir Vovk, Alex Gammerman, and Glenn Shafer (Springer, 2005).

resources.title: Estimating diagnostic uncertainty in artificial intelligence assisted pathology using conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Unreliable predictions can occur when an artificial intelligence (AI) system is presented with data it has not been exposed to during training. We demonstrate the use of conformal prediction to detect unreliable predictions, using histopathological diagnosis and grading of prostate biopsies as example. We digitized 7788 prostate biopsies from 1192 men in the STHLM3 diagnostic study, used for training, and 3059 biopsies from 676 men used for testing. With conformal prediction, 1 in 794 (0.1%) predictions is incorrect for cancer diagnosis (compared to 14 errors [2%] without conformal prediction) while 175 (22%) of the predictions are flagged as unreliable when the AI-system is presented with new data from the same lab and scanner that it was trained on. Conformal prediction could with small samples ( N = 49 for external scanner, N = 10 for external lab and scanner, and N = 12 for external lab, scanner and pathology assessment) detect systematic differences in external data leading to worse predictive performance. The AI-system with conformal prediction commits 3 (2%) errors for cancer detection in cases of atypical prostate tissue compared to 44 (25%) without conformal prediction, while the system flags 143 (80%) unreliable predictions. We conclude that conformal prediction can increase patient safety of AI-systems.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out test set from the same patient population as the calibration data, the 95% prediction sets contained the true diagnosis in at least 95% of cases, within sampling error.
Prediction-set coverage on the latest quarter of live data stays within the agreed margin of its nominal level, so there is no sign that the exchangeability assumption has broken down in deployment.

For the perception model, the 95% prediction sets contained the true object class in at least 95% of held-out frames, and frames whose set holds more than one class trigger the cautious fallback behaviour.
Every credit-limit recommendation is shown with a set of plausible limit bands at 90% coverage, and any case whose set holds more than one band is routed to a human underwriter.

The 90% prediction sets are calibrated separately within each demographic group, and on held-out cases their coverage is within three percentage points of 90% in every group, with each group's number of calibration and test cases reported.

techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

resources.title: Assessing calibration and bias of a deployed machine learning malnutrition prediction model within a large healthcare system
resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

sample_claims.text: After Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes, the default model's predicted probabilities agree with observed default rates in every score decile, within the tolerance set in the model risk policy.

After Platt scaling, the defect classifier's log loss on the held-out test set is lower than before, and its reliability diagram shows predicted defect rates within the tolerance set in the quality plan.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

sample_claims.text: On a test set not used to fit the temperature, the diagnostic model's expected calibration error is below the agreed threshold, and observed accuracy in each confidence band is within tolerance of its stated confidence.

Calibrating the credit risk model with a single temperature left its predicted classes, and therefore its accuracy, unchanged, while its default probabilities now track the observed default rates on held-out data.
A displayed confidence of 80% corresponds to about 80 correct predictions in 100, as shown by a reliability diagram on data not used to fit the temperature.
After refitting the temperature on a labelled sample from the new region, the land-cover classifier's calibration error on that region's test data is no worse than on the original region.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

Uncertainty-aware body composition analysis with deep regression ensembles on UK Biobank MRI
resources.abstract: Along with rich health-related metadata, medical images have been acquired for over 40,000 male and female UK Biobank participants, aged 44-82, since 2014. Phenotypes derived from these images, such as measurements of body composition from MRI, can reveal new links between genetics, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic conditions. In this work, six measurements of body composition and adipose tissues were automatically estimated by image-based, deep regression with ResNet50 neural networks from neck-to-knee body MRI. Despite the potential for high speed and accuracy, these networks produce no output segmentations that could indicate the reliability of individual measurements. The presented experiments therefore examine uncertainty quantification with mean-variance regression and ensembling to estimate individual measurement errors and thereby identify potential outliers, anomalies, and other failure cases automatically. In 10-fold cross-validation on data of about 8500 subjects, mean-variance regression and ensembling showed complementary benefits, reducing the mean absolute error across all predictions by 12%. Both improved the calibration of uncertainties and their ability to identify high prediction errors. With intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) above 0.97, all targets except the liver fat content yielded relative measurement errors below 5%. Testing on another 1000 subjects showed consistent performance, and the method was finally deployed for inference to 30,000 subjects with missing reference values. The results indicate that deep regression ensembles could ultimately provide automated, uncertainty-aware measurements of body composition for more than 120,000 UK Biobank neck-to-knee body MRI that are to be acquired within the coming years.

sample_claims.text: On held-out scans, the imaging model's ensemble uncertainty is higher for cases it gets wrong than for cases it gets right, so scans above the uncertainty threshold can be sent for manual review.
The ensemble's predicted probabilities are calibrated on held-out data, so that predictions made with 90% confidence are correct about 90% of the time.
When shown inputs from a class absent from the training data, the ensemble's disagreement is measurably higher than on in-distribution inputs, as tested on a held-out set of unseen-class examples.

The driving system reports an uncertainty level with each detection, derived from disagreement between independently trained networks, and remote operators are alerted when it passes the documented limit.
Each credit score shown to underwriters carries an uncertainty range from the ensemble, and scores with a wide range are labelled as low-confidence.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Ensembles
techniques.description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

example_use_cases.description: An electricity network operator forecasting next-day demand at each substation trains 100 gradient-boosted models on bootstrap replicates of three years of meter readings, resampled in whole-week blocks because consecutive readings are correlated. Planners hold extra reserve at substations where the models' forecasts spread widely, because those are the sites whose forecasts the historical data settle least.

A hospital's readmission-risk tool shows clinicians, beside each patient's predicted risk, the range of risks given by models trained on bootstrap replicates of the training cohort, resampling patients rather than admissions so that one patient's admissions stay together, so that a clinician can see when an estimate rests on few comparable past patients and give it less weight in discharge planning.

A local authority reviewing a housing-need scoring model compares the average spread of bootstrap-ensemble scores across applicant groups and finds it widest for a group with few past applications, which shows that the model's scores for that group are least settled by the data; it collects more cases before letting the scores inform priority for that group.

limitations.description: Every member of the ensemble is a full training run, and every prediction must be made by every member, so training cost, storage and prediction time all grow in proportion to the number of replicates. For large neural networks this usually limits the ensemble to a handful of members, too few for stable percentiles of the spread.

The spread measures uncertainty in the fitted model, not the noise in outcomes. Presented as the range within which a case's actual outcome will fall, it understates the uncertainty, most of all where outcomes are noisy and training data plentiful, so the outcome noise has to be estimated separately, for example from held-out errors, and added.

The spread reflects only what the procedure lets vary: which cases are in each training set and, for models trained from a random start such as neural networks, each member's starting point. Fixed choices such as features, architecture and training settings add no spread. A model consistently wrong for a group the data under-represent can show little spread there, and members can agree closely on inputs unlike the training data, so a small spread is not evidence of reliability.

Each replicate contains on average only about 63 per cent of the distinct training cases, so each member learns from less information than a model trained on all the data. With small datasets or rare classes, some replicates may contain almost none of a rare class or subgroup, which inflates the spread for those cases and can leave individual members unusable.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. With repeated measurements of the same person, time series or other grouped data, case resampling spreads related cases across replicates and understates the uncertainty, unless whole groups or time blocks are resampled instead.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

The  confidence  interval  follows  from the variation in an ensemble of neural networks,  each of them  trained and stopped on bootstrap replicates of the original data set.  A second improvement is the use of the residuals on validation pat(cid:173) terns  instead of on training patterns for  estimation of the variance  of the  target  distribution.  As  illustrated  on  a  synthetic  example,  our method is  better than existing methods with regard to extrap(cid:173) olation and interpolation in data regimes with a limited amount of  data, and yields prediction intervals which  actual confidence  levels  are closer  to the desired  confidence  levels.

sample_claims.text: For each substation's next-day demand forecast, the spread across models trained on bootstrap replicates of the historical data, resampled in whole-week blocks, is reported, and forecasts whose spread exceeds the planning tolerance are flagged.
The flood model's uncertainty for each river gauge reflects how much its predictions change when it is retrained on versions of the gauge records resampled in blocks of consecutive days.
Each readmission-risk score shown to clinicians is accompanied by the range of scores produced by models trained on resampled versions of the training cohort.
The spread of the housing-need model's scores across bootstrap-trained models has been compared between applicant groups and is reported for each group.

techniques.name: Jackknife Resampling
techniques.description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data team fits a readmission-risk model on 600 patient records and refits it 600 times, leaving out one patient each time. The spread of the refitted coefficients shows which risk factors are stable enough to report, and the records whose removal shifts the fit most go back to clinicians to check for entry errors.

A water utility's analysts estimate how rainfall drives reservoir inflow from 40 annual observations. Leaving out each year in turn gives a variance estimate for the fitted slope and shows whether a single flood year drives the result, before the figure goes into a planning document.

A credit-risk team documents its scorecard's stability for model validators by refitting it with each of 800 sampled loan records left out. It reports the records whose removal changes any coefficient by more than a stated tolerance, so validators can see how much of the model rests on a few loans.

limitations.description: Computationally heavy when the result needs a model refit, since n records mean n refits, which is impractical for datasets with thousands or millions of records or for costly training. Simple statistics that are cheap to recompute do not have this problem.

Works only for statistics that change smoothly when one record is removed. For quantities that jump, such as the number of clusters in a mixture model, leave-one-out estimates are unreliable. Even for smooth statistics the variance estimate tends to run high, so intervals are conservative.

Assumes the records are independent. With repeated or clustered measurements, such as several visits per patient or neighbouring regions, leaving out one record leaves its close relatives in the data, so the refits barely change and the spread understates the true uncertainty.
Provides limited insight into model behaviour on truly novel data, as each jackknife sample is only minimally different from the full training set.

Measures how sensitive a result is to the sample in hand, not whether the model is right. A stable fit can still be systematically wrong, so a narrow spread across refits is no evidence of accuracy, or of performance on a different population.

sample_claims.text: The readmission model's coefficient estimates change by less than a stated tolerance when any single patient record is removed, so no individual record drives the reported risk factors.
The jackknife standard error of the fitted rainfall-to-inflow slope is reported with the estimate, and the planning threshold lies more than two standard errors away from it.
The scorecard's validation report lists the loan records whose removal most changes its coefficients, so reviewers can see how far the model depends on a handful of loans.

techniques.name: Cross-validation
techniques.description: Cross-validation estimates how well a model will perform on data it has not seen, and how much that estimate depends on the particular data used. The dataset is divided into k parts called folds, the model is trained on all but one fold and scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats until every fold has served as the held-out set once. The scores are averaged to give a performance estimate, and their spread gives a rough indication of how much the result depends on which data the model was trained on. Common variants are stratified cross-validation, where each fold keeps the overall class proportions, and leave-one-out, where each fold is a single example. A large gap between training scores and held-out scores points to overfitting, where a model has learned quirks of its training data that do not carry over to new data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data-science team has records for about 900 patients and is building a readmission-risk model. It runs 10-fold cross-validation with each patient's admissions kept in the same fold, then reports the mean and spread of held-out scores. A wide spread, or a large gap to the training score, tells the team the model is not yet stable enough to take to a prospective trial.

A bank's fraud team compares three candidate classifiers by running the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation on a year of labelled transactions, so every candidate is scored on identical folds and the rare fraud cases are spread evenly across them. They select the model with the best mean recall at a fixed false-alarm rate and drop any candidate whose fold-to-fold scores vary widely.

A materials-science group has only 120 labelled samples from costly experiments. Instead of trusting one train-test split, it repeats 5-fold cross-validation with different random splits and reports the spread of the accuracy estimate, which decides whether the model is reliable enough to guide the next round of experiments.

limitations.description: The number of folds trades cost against bias and variance. Each fold is another training run. Few folds (2 to 5) train on less data and tend to understate performance, whereas leave-one-out has little bias but unstable estimates and the highest cost. Ten folds is a common compromise, not a rule.

Assumes records are independent. If the same patient, customer or site appears in several records, a fold can be trained on records nearly identical to those it is tested on, and the score is optimistic. Folds must then be built by group, not drawn at random.

Ignores time order. Training on later records and testing on earlier ones lets future information leak into the estimate and flatters the model. For time-ordered data, use an evaluation that always tests on data later than the training data, such as rolling-origin evaluation.

Anything learned from the data must be fitted inside each training fold, including scaling, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Done once on the full dataset beforehand, it leaks test-fold information and inflates the scores. Tuning and reporting on the same folds is also optimistic, so nested cross-validation is needed for both.

A score from a small sample is imprecise, and the spread across folds understates the true uncertainty. In one neuroimaging study, error bars on a cross-validated score were roughly plus or minus 10% with 100 samples, so a small gain between two models can be noise.

resources.title: Cross-validation failure: Small sample sizes lead to large error bars
resources.abstract: Predictive models ground many state‐of‐the‐art developments in statistical brain image analysis: decoding, MVPA, searchlight, or extraction of biomarkers. The principled approach to establish their validity and usefulness is cross‐validation, testing prediction on unseen data. Here, I would like to raise awareness on error bars of cross‐validation, which are often underestimated. Simple experiments show that sample sizes of many neuroimaging studies inherently lead to large error bars, eg Symbol for 100 samples. The standard error across folds strongly underestimates them. These large error bars compromise the reliability of conclusions drawn with predictive models, such as biomarkers or methods developments where, unlike with cognitive neuroimaging MVPA approaches, more samples cannot be acquired by repeating the experiment across many subjects. Solutions to increase sample size must be investigated, tackling possible increases in heterogeneity of the data.

techniques.name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
techniques.description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. Neither precision nor recall uses true negatives, so a large majority class does not flatter the score as it can flatter accuracy and AUC-ROC. A model with no skill scores about the proportion of positives in the data, so the score is only meaningful next to that baseline.

example_use_cases.description: A payments team compares candidate fraud models on a held-out month of transactions in which about 1 in 500 is fraudulent. It ranks them by AUPRC against the 0.2% no-skill baseline, then reads the best model's curve to choose a threshold that keeps false alarms within what the investigation team can review.

A hospital evaluates a model that screens for a rare condition affecting about 1 in 200 patients. ROC AUC can look high even when most flagged patients are healthy, so the team reports AUPRC against the 0.5% baseline and reads the precision at the recall clinicians require, to decide whether the follow-up workload is manageable.

A manufacturer compares two defect-detection models for a production line where about 1 in 1,000 parts is faulty. It uses AUPRC on a labelled validation batch to choose between them, so that a model is not preferred simply for labelling nearly every good part correctly.

limitations.description: AUPRC depends on the share of positives in the data, so scores from datasets or groups with different proportions cannot be compared directly, and no universal pass mark can be set. Each score has to be read against its own no-skill baseline, which is about the positive proportion.

It treats one class as the positive class and ignores true negatives, so it says nothing about how reliably the model clears the majority class. That matters where certifying a case as negative or safe is as important as catching positives.

A single area averages over every threshold, including ones no deployment would use, and can hide poor precision at the recall the application needs. Choosing the operating point needs a look at that part of the curve and the cost of each kind of error.

The area can be computed in different ways. Trapezoidal linear interpolation between points gives an overly optimistic value, whereas step-wise average precision does not, so scores from different libraries or settings may not match.
Few positive test cases make precision-recall estimates unstable, so a high score from a small sample may not hold on a larger, representative evaluation set.

resources.title: The relationship between Precision-Recall and ROC curves
resources.abstract: Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curves are commonly used to present results for binary decision problems in machine learning. However, when dealing with highly skewed datasets, Precision-Recall (PR) curves give a more informative picture of an algorithm's performance. We show that a deep connection exists between ROC space and PR space, such that a curve dominates in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space. A corollary is the notion of an achievable PR curve, which has properties much like the convex hull in ROC space; we show an efficient algorithm for computing this curve. Finally, we also note differences in the two types of curves are significant for algorithm design. For example, in PR space it is incorrect to linearly interpolate between points. Furthermore, algorithms that optimize the area under the ROC curve are not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve.

techniques.name: Safety Envelope Testing
techniques.description: Safety envelope testing checks how an AI system performs at and beyond the edges of the conditions it was designed for, so that failure modes are found before deployment. Testers first write down those conditions, called the operational design domain, such as the road types, weather, lighting and speeds a vehicle is built for. They then build scenarios that push each condition towards its limit and past it, and measure how performance degrades as conditions get harder, repeating runs where the system does not behave the same way twice. The results show where, within the conditions tested, the system moves from acceptable to unsafe behaviour. They support operating limits, safety margins and a point at which the system should hand over to a person or stop.

example_use_cases.description: Testing autonomous vehicle perception systems at the limits of weather conditions, lighting, and sensor coverage to establish safe operational boundaries and determine when human intervention is required.

A radiology team tests a chest X-ray triage model on scans at the edge of its intended use, such as the poorest image quality and the oldest scanner models it was approved for, and records where sensitivity falls below the agreed floor, so that scans beyond that point are referred to a radiologist.

A trading firm replays historical crash periods and synthetic shocks with volatility pushed beyond the range its trading model was developed on, to check that position limits and the automatic trading halt trigger before losses reach the agreed ceiling.

limitations.description: Results are only as good as the operational design domain used. If the specification omits a condition the system meets in service, such as a road type or a market regime, the tests probe the wrong edge and a clean result gives false confidence.

Coverage is incomplete by construction. Conditions interact across many dimensions, so the number of boundary combinations grows quickly, and failures that appear only when several factors reach their limits together can be missed.
Performance of a learned system need not fall smoothly towards the boundary. Failures can sit inside the envelope, so good results at the edge do not show that the interior is safe.

Results describe one system version in one test setting, and a single pass proves little for a system that behaves differently on successive runs, which needs repeated trials. Retraining, new sensors or a gap between simulation and the real world can move the boundary, so the tests need repeating after each material change.
The technique shows where the system stops performing acceptably. It does not keep the system inside that envelope in service, which needs a separate runtime monitor or out-of-distribution detector.

resources.title: BS ISO 34503:2023 Road vehicles. Test scenarios for automated driving systems. Specification for operational design domain
Challenges in Autonomous Vehicle Testing and Validation
resources.abstract: Software testing is all too often simply a bug hunt rather than a well-considered exercise in ensuring quality. A more methodical approach than a simple cycle of system-level test-fail-patch-test will be required to deploy safe autonomous vehicles at scale. The ISO 26262 development V process sets up a framework that ties each type of testing to a corresponding design or requirement document, but presents challenges when adapted to deal with the sorts of novel testing problems that face autonomous vehicles. This paper identifies five major challenge areas in testing according to the V model for autonomous vehicles: driver out of the loop, complex requirements, non-deterministic algorithms, inductive learning algorithms, and fail-operational systems. General solution approaches that seem promising across these different challenge areas include: phased deployment using successively relaxed operational scenarios, use of a monitor/actuator pair architecture to separate the most complex autonomy functions from simpler safety functions, and fault injection as a way to perform more efficient edge case testing. While significant challenges remain in safety-certifying the type of algorithms that provide high-level autonomy themselves, it seems within reach to instead architect the system and its accompanying design process to be able to employ existing software safety approaches.

resources.title: System and Safety Analysis for Autonomous Center-line Tracking with SYSAI
resources.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2022-2399.vid Machine learning (ML) applications and Artificial Intelligence (AI) components have become increasingly important in the Aerospace domain. However, traditional assurance processes and tools are not well suited for the Verification and Validation (V&V) of safety-critical systems with AI components. In this paper, we present SYSAI (System Analysis using Statistical AI), a flexible statistical learning framework for the V&V and analysis of complex and high-dimensional Aerospace systems with Neural Network components. SYSAI provides functionality for numerous analysis and V&V tasks, including statistical analysis of training data, safety-envelope and time-series analysis, property checking, and intelligent test-case generation. We demonstrate SYSAI with our industrial partner’s ACT (Autonomous Centerline Tracking) component.

techniques.name: Red Teaming
techniques.description: Red teaming is a structured adversarial evaluation process in which a dedicated team systematically probes an AI/ML system to discover vulnerabilities and failure modes. Unlike individual testing techniques (such as prompt injection testing, jailbreak resistance testing, or safety envelope testing), red teaming defines the organisational methodology: team composition, campaign planning, attack taxonomy, and reporting structure. The red team coordinates diverse attack vectors — including prompt manipulation, adversarial examples, edge case exploitation, and social engineering scenarios — into a coherent assessment programme. Results feed into risk registers and remediation plans rather than pass/fail metrics.

example_use_cases.description: Testing a content moderation AI by attempting to make it generate harmful outputs through creative prompt injection, jailbreaking techniques, and edge case scenarios to identify safety vulnerabilities before deployment.

Probing a medical diagnosis AI system with adversarial examples and edge cases to identify failure modes that could lead to incorrect diagnoses, ensuring the system fails gracefully rather than confidently providing wrong information.

Systematically testing a hiring algorithm with inputs designed to reveal hidden biases, using adversarial examples to check if the system can be manipulated to discriminate against protected groups or favour certain demographics unfairly.

Systematically testing AI systems for security vulnerabilities including prompt injection, data exfiltration, jailbreaking, and model manipulation by simulating adversarial attacks. This helps identify security weaknesses before deployment and provides documented evidence for compliance with regulatory requirements such as EU AI Act Article 55 and ISO 42001 adversarial testing mandates.

limitations.description: Requires highly specialized expertise in both AI/ML systems and adversarial attack methods, making it expensive and difficult to scale across organizations.
Limited by the creativity and knowledge of red team members - can only discover vulnerabilities that testers think to explore, potentially missing novel attack vectors.
Time-intensive process that may not be feasible for rapid development cycles or resource-constrained projects, potentially delaying beneficial system deployments.
May not generalize to real-world adversarial scenarios, as red team attacks may differ significantly from actual malicious use patterns or user behaviours.
Risk of false confidence if red teaming is incomplete or superficial, leading organizations to believe systems are safer than they actually are.

resources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
resources.abstract: We describe our early efforts to red team language models in order to simultaneously discover, measure, and attempt to reduce their potentially harmful outputs. We make three main contributions. First, we investigate scaling behaviors for red teaming across 3 model sizes (2.7B, 13B, and 52B parameters) and 4 model types: a plain language model (LM); an LM prompted to be helpful, honest, and harmless; an LM with rejection sampling; and a model trained to be helpful and harmless using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). We find that the RLHF models are increasingly difficult to red team as they scale, and we find a flat trend with scale for the other model types. Second, we release our dataset of 38,961 red team attacks for others to analyze and learn from. We provide our own analysis of the data and find a variety of harmful outputs, which range from offensive language to more subtly harmful non-violent unethical outputs. Third, we exhaustively describe our instructions, processes, statistical methodologies, and uncertainty about red teaming. We hope that this transparency accelerates our ability to work together as a community in order to develop shared norms, practices, and technical standards for how to red team language models.

resources.title: Red Teaming LLM Applications - DeepLearning.AI
Red teaming ChatGPT in medicine to yield real-world insights on model behavior
resources.abstract: Red teaming, the practice of adversarially exposing unexpected or undesired model behaviors, is critical towards improving equity and accuracy of large language models, but non-model creator-affiliated red teaming is scant in healthcare. We convened teams of clinicians, medical and engineering students, and technical professionals (80 participants total) to stress-test models with real-world clinical cases and categorize inappropriate responses along axes of safety, privacy, hallucinations/accuracy, and bias. Six medically-trained reviewers re-analyzed prompt-response pairs and added qualitative annotations. Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%). Subsequently, we show the utility of our benchmark by testing GPT-4o, a model released after our event (20.4% inappropriate). 21.5% of responses appropriate with GPT-3.5 were inappropriate in updated models. We share insights for constructing red teaming prompts, and present our benchmark for iterative model assessments.

techniques.name: Model Cards
techniques.description: Model cards are standardised documentation frameworks that systematically document machine learning models through structured templates. The templates cover intended use cases, performance metrics across different demographic groups and operating conditions, training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, limitations, and ethical considerations. They serve as comprehensive technical specifications that enable informed model selection, prevent inappropriate deployment, support regulatory compliance, and facilitate fair assessment by providing transparent reporting of model capabilities and constraints across diverse populations and scenarios.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Creating comprehensive model cards for hiring algorithms that transparently report performance differences across demographic groups, helping HR departments identify potential bias issues and ensure equitable candidate evaluation processes.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

limitations.description: Creating comprehensive model cards requires substantial time, expertise, and resources to gather performance data across diverse conditions and demographic groups, potentially delaying model deployment timelines.
Information can become outdated quickly as models are retrained, updated, or deployed in new contexts, requiring ongoing maintenance and version control to remain accurate and useful.
Organisations may provide incomplete or superficial documentation to avoid revealing competitive advantages or potential liabilities, undermining the transparency goals of model cards.
Lack of standardised formats and enforcement mechanisms means model card quality and completeness vary significantly across different organisations and use cases.
Technical complexity of documenting model behaviour across all relevant dimensions may exceed the expertise of some development teams, leading to gaps in critical information.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.abstract: Trained machine learning models are increasingly used to perform high-impact tasks in areas such as law enforcement, medicine, education, and employment. In order to clarify the intended use cases of machine learning models and minimize their usage in contexts for which they are not well suited, we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics. In this paper, we propose a framework that we call model cards, to encourage such transparent model reporting. Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups (e.g., race, geographic location, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type) and intersectional groups (e.g., age and race, or sex and Fitzpatrick skin type) that are relevant to the intended application domains. Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information. While we focus primarily on human-centered machine learning models in the application fields of computer vision and natural language processing, this framework can be used to document any trained machine learning model. To solidify the concept, we provide cards for two supervised models: One trained to detect smiling faces in images, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text. We propose model cards as a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning and related AI technology, increasing transparency into how well AI technology works. We hope this work encourages those releasing trained machine learning models to accompany model releases with similar detailed evaluation numbers and other relevant documentation.

resources.title: Systematic analysis of 32,111 AI model cards characterizes documentation practice in AI
Interactive Model Cards: A Human-Centered Approach to Model Documentation
resources.abstract: Deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly adopted and deployed by analysts without formal training in NLP or machine learning (ML). However, the documentation intended to convey the model’s details and appropriate use is tailored primarily to individuals with ML or NLP expertise. To address this gap, we conduct a design inquiry into interactive model cards, which augment traditionally static model cards with affordances for exploring model documentation and interacting with the models themselves. Our investigation consists of an initial conceptual study with experts in ML, NLP, and AI Ethics, followed by a separate evaluative study with non-expert analysts who use ML models in their work. Using a semi-structured interview format coupled with a think-aloud protocol, we collected feedback from a total of 30 participants who engaged with different versions of standard and interactive model cards. Through a thematic analysis of the collected data, we identified several conceptual dimensions that summarize the strengths and limitations of standard and interactive model cards, including: stakeholders; design; guidance; understandability & interpretability; sensemaking & skepticism; and trust & safety. Our findings demonstrate the importance of carefully considered design and interactivity for orienting and supporting non-expert analysts using deep learning models, along with a need for consideration of broader sociotechnical contexts and organizational dynamics. We have also identified design elements, such as language, visual cues, and warnings, among others, that support interactivity and make non-interactive content accessible. We summarize our findings as design guidelines and discuss their implications for a human-centered approach towards AI/ML documentation.

techniques.name: Datasheets for Datasets
techniques.description: Datasheets for datasets establish comprehensive documentation standards for datasets, systematically recording creation methodology, data composition, collection procedures, preprocessing transformations, intended applications, potential biases, privacy considerations, and maintenance protocols. These structured documents enhance dataset transparency by providing essential context for appropriate usage, enabling informed decisions about dataset suitability for specific tasks, supporting bias detection and mitigation efforts, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations, and promoting responsible data stewardship throughout the entire data lifecycle from collection to disposal.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical imaging dataset with detailed information about patient privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and data sharing constraints to ensure sensitive health information is handled appropriately and regulatory compliance is maintained.

Creating comprehensive datasheets for recruitment datasets that document demographic representation across different job categories, helping developers identify potential bias in training data and develop more equitable hiring algorithms.

Establishing transparent documentation for financial transaction datasets that clearly describes data collection methodology, preprocessing steps, and intended use cases, enabling researchers to make informed decisions about dataset appropriateness for their specific applications.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

Documenting the statistical distributions, temporal coverage, and known quality characteristics of training datasets to support model monitoring pipelines, enabling operations teams to detect data drift and assess whether production data remains within the documented training distribution for informed decisions about model retraining or recalibration.

limitations.description: Creating thorough datasheets requires significant time investment and domain expertise to properly document collection methods, biases, and ethical considerations, potentially delaying dataset release or publication.
Information may become outdated as datasets undergo preprocessing, cleaning, or augmentation, requiring ongoing maintenance to ensure documentation accuracy throughout the data lifecycle.
Absence of standardised templates and enforcement mechanisms leads to inconsistent documentation quality and completeness across different organisations and research communities.
Dataset creators may intentionally omit sensitive information about collection methods, participant consent, or potential biases to avoid legal liability or competitive disadvantage.
Limited adoption and awareness means many existing datasets lack proper documentation, creating gaps in the historical record and making legacy dataset assessment difficult.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.abstract: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. To address this gap, we propose datasheets for datasets. In the electronics industry, every component, no matter how simple or complex, is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information. By analogy, we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning Practitioners' Data Documentation Perceptions, Needs, Challenges, and Desiderata
resources.abstract: Data is central to the development and evaluation of machine learning (ML) models. However, the use of problematic or inappropriate datasets can result in harms when the resulting models are deployed. To encourage responsible AI practice through more deliberate reflection on datasets and transparency around the processes by which they are created, researchers and practitioners have begun to advocate for increased data documentation and have proposed several data documentation frameworks. However, there is little research on whether these data documentation frameworks meet the needs of ML practitioners, who both create and consume datasets. To address this gap, we set out to understand ML practitioners' data documentation perceptions, needs, challenges, and desiderata, with the goal of deriving design requirements that can inform future data documentation frameworks. We conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 14 ML practitioners at a single large, international technology company. We had them answer a list of questions taken from datasheets for datasets (Gebru, 2021). Our findings show that current approaches to data documentation are largely ad hoc and myopic in nature. Participants expressed needs for data documentation frameworks to be adaptable to their contexts, integrated into their existing tools and workflows, and automated wherever possible. Despite the fact that data documentation frameworks are often motivated from the perspective of responsible AI, participants did not make the connection between the questions that they were asked to answer and their responsible AI implications. In addition, participants often had difficulties prioritizing the needs of dataset consumers and providing information that someone unfamiliar with their datasets might need to know. Based on these findings, we derive seven design requirements for future data documentation frameworks.
