techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

techniques.name: AutoAttack
techniques.description: AutoAttack is a fixed suite of four automated adversarial attacks, introduced by Croce and Hein (ICML 2020), that measures how much of an image classifier's test accuracy survives small, deliberately chosen changes to its input images at inference time. The evaluator states the threat model, a norm and radius that bound the change (for example, no pixel value changed by more than 8/255 under the L-infinity norm), and the standard version then attacks each correctly classified test image in turn with APGD-CE (projected gradient descent that sets its own step size, on the cross-entropy loss), a targeted APGD on the authors' Difference of Logits Ratio loss, a targeted form of the FAB minimum-norm attack, and the Square Attack, which needs only the model's outputs and so still works when gradients are uninformative. An image counts as robust only if none of the four finds a misclassified version within the bound, and because every attack setting is fixed in advance the evaluator tunes nothing, which removes a common cause of overstated robustness: an attack too weakly tuned for the model. The output is robust accuracy, the share of test images still classified correctly under attack at the stated norm and radius, reported beside clean accuracy; published models are compared on the RobustBench leaderboard, which uses AutoAttack as its standard evaluation. Because AutoAttack is not built around any one defence, it can supply the attack step for a wider judgement of a defence, such as whether adversarial training holds up against attacks it was not trained on; unlike red teaming, it involves no human attacker or open-ended search.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team validating a vendor's classifier that recognises which of 40 identity-document types a customer has photographed during remote account opening, so the right authenticity checks run, receives the model weights under the review agreement. It reruns the vendor's robustness evaluation with standard AutoAttack at the same L-infinity radius, compares the two robust accuracies and records any automatic warnings before accepting the vendor's figure.

A photo-sharing platform's trust-and-safety team expects uploaders to perturb images to slip past the classifier that sorts uploads into a dozen prohibited-content categories and an allowed class. Choosing between two candidate models, it runs standard AutoAttack on both at a perturbation budget agreed with its security team, and selects the one with higher robust accuracy whose clean-accuracy cost is acceptable, recording both figures in the release review.

A research group proposing a new defence for a traffic-sign classifier runs standard AutoAttack before publication and finds that the Square Attack lowers robust accuracy further than the gradient-based attacks, one of AutoAttack's warning signs that gradients are masked. It treats its figure as an upper bound and has an attack designed for its defence built before claiming any robustness.

A computational-pathology group comparing a convolutional network and a vision transformer for three-way tumour subtyping on routine slide images attacks both with AutoAttack, its settings reduced for three classes, at several perturbation sizes below what a blinded clinical reader could detect, and compares attack success rates on an external patient cohort to decide which architecture goes forward.

limitations.description: Robust accuracy from AutoAttack is an upper bound: an image counts as robust because these four attacks failed, not because no adversarial example exists. The authors present it as the minimum test for a new defence rather than the strongest possible attack, so a claim that no change within the bound can alter a decision needs a certified-robustness method instead.

The standard version can overstate robustness for defences that are randomised, not differentiable or run an optimisation loop at inference. The reference code warns about some of these cases, offers a version averaging gradients over the model's randomness, and recommends attacks built for the specific defence; RobustBench excludes such defences. A defence tuned to beat AutoAttack itself can pass it without being robust.

The result holds only for the norm and radius tested. It gives no direct evidence about patches, rotations, physical changes to objects or natural corruptions: in RobustBench's quick-start guide, L-infinity-robust models do much worse than an undefended model on fog-corrupted images, though better on average across corruption types. Benchmark radii such as 8/255 are conventions, so the radius should be justified from the deployment's threat, and a new norm or radius needs a new run.

It needs white-box access: three of the four attacks use the model's gradients, and the code expects raw scores (logits) and inputs scaled to [0, 1]; with access only to output scores, the Square Attack can run alone, a weaker test. The standard settings also assume ten or more classes, since the targeted attacks each try nine other classes; on a binary or few-class model the reference code stops with an error, so the settings must be reduced and the result is no longer the standard one.

The full evaluation is computationally heavy for large models and test sets: each white-box run uses 100 iterations, the targeted attacks each try nine target classes, and the Square Attack makes up to 5,000 queries per image. RobustBench's quick start runs a cheaper two-attack version on 50 images and notes the full version is slower but more accurate; a figure from a subset should be reported with its sampling error.

resources.title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks
resources.abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10\%$, identifying several broken defenses.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

resources.title: Private Ad Modeling with DP-SGD
resources.abstract: A well-known algorithm in privacy-preserving ML is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). While this algorithm has been evaluated on text and image data, it has not been previously applied to ads data, which are notorious for their high class imbalance and sparse gradient updates. In this work we apply DP-SGD to several ad modeling tasks including predicting click-through rates, conversion rates, and number of conversion events, and evaluate their privacy-utility trade-off on real-world datasets. Our work is the first to empirically demonstrate that DP-SGD can provide both privacy and utility for ad modeling tasks.

sample_claims.text: The credit-default model shared with the partner lender was trained with DP-SGD to epsilon 2 and delta 10^-7, with each customer contributing one training example and the budget computed over every training step by the accountant in Opacus.

The published chest X-ray model weights satisfy differential privacy with epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5 with respect to any one patient, and the hyperparameter search run on patient images is included in that budget.
Training batches were drawn by Poisson sampling, matching the assumption of the privacy accountant that produced the reported epsilon.
The skills-tagging model's privacy budget of epsilon 4 per applicant covers the full fine-tuning run and every hyperparameter trial run on applicants' CVs.

techniques.name: k-Anonymity
techniques.description: k-Anonymity is a property that a table of real records about people can be made to satisfy before it is released or shared, in which every record shares its values on the quasi-identifiers with at least k-1 other records, so anyone linking the table to another source on those columns always matches a group of at least k records, which is k people only when each person has one record. Quasi-identifiers are columns that are not names or ID numbers but could be found elsewhere and combined to single a person out, such as date of birth, sex and postcode, and because the data holder chooses them, the protection covers only those columns. To reach a chosen k, each quasi-identifier is coarsened along a hierarchy set in advance (exact age to five-year band, full postcode to district), and the values or records that would still sit in a group smaller than k are suppressed, with a search choosing the coarsening that loses least information. The output is the transformed table of real records made less specific, not artificial ones, together with the k it achieves and a measure of the detail lost. Unlike differential privacy, it gives no bound on what an observer can learn, because it blocks linking on the listed columns but does not stop someone learning a sensitive value that everyone in a group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust preparing an extract of emergency attendances for a university research team treats age, sex, postcode district and attendance date as quasi-identifiers, since local news reports and social media posts about incidents often carry them. Using ARX it generalises age to five-year bands and dates to weeks, suppresses the records still in groups smaller than five, and sends the extract with a note of the k achieved, the columns covered and the share of records suppressed.

A national statistics office preparing a scientific-use file of a household survey for registered researchers recodes region and occupation into broader groups in sdcMicro, then applies local suppression until every combination of age band, sex, region and household size occurs at least three times, and publishes the number of suppressed values with the file so that users can judge the effect on their analyses.

A motor insurer sharing a claims table with an analytics firm that will build a fraud-detection model applies 10-anonymity to policyholder age, vehicle model and postcode district. Before release it agrees with the firm that the coarser bands still carry enough signal for the model, and it keeps the generalisation scheme so that later releases are generalised from the same scheme rather than a new one.

limitations.description: k-Anonymity hides which record is a person's, not what their group has in common. If all k records in a group share the same diagnosis, anyone who can place a person in that group learns the diagnosis, and an attacker with extra background knowledge can rule out other members of the group. Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness add conditions on the sensitive column for this reason; k-anonymity alone does not prevent sensitive values being disclosed.

The protection covers only the columns the data holder lists as quasi-identifiers, and rests on the holder judging correctly which columns an attacker could find elsewhere. A column left off the list, such as a rare diagnosis that a local newspaper has reported, can still single a record out, and the property says nothing about it. Choosing the list needs a realistic picture of the public, commercial and leaked data an attacker could hold.

Each release is protected only on its own. Two k-anonymous versions of the same data, generalised differently or produced at different times as records are added, can be joined to narrow groups below k, and two releases that keep the rows in the same order can be lined up row by row. Later releases must be built from the first, or treat all its released columns as quasi-identifiers, and row order must be randomised before each release.

With many quasi-identifiers or detailed values such as exact dates and measurements, most records are unique, and reaching k needs coarsening or suppression heavy enough to remove the detail an analysis or model depends on; the method suits continuous variables poorly. Because the suppressed records are those with rare combinations of values, the released table can under-represent exactly the unusual cases a model most needs to handle.

Requiring k within the released table treats the attacker as knowing their target is in it. When the table is a small sample of a larger population, a record unique in the table may match many people outside it, so the requirement over-protects; El Emam and Dankar found this over-anonymisation, and the loss of information it causes, greatest at small sampling fractions. A re-identification risk assessment against the population can justify a lighter transformation.

techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

techniques.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
techniques.description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

resources.title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
resources.abstract: To understand the risks posed by a new AI system, we must understand what it can and cannot do. Building on prior work, we introduce a programme of new "dangerous capability" evaluations and pilot them on Gemini 1.0 models. Our evaluations cover four areas: (1) persuasion and deception; (2) cyber-security; (3) self-proliferation; and (4) self-reasoning. We do not find evidence of strong dangerous capabilities in the models we evaluated, but we flag early warning signs. Our goal is to help advance a rigorous science of dangerous capability evaluation, in preparation for future models.

techniques.name: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
techniques.description: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (ML FMEA) applies the process form of failure mode and effects analysis, a long-established worksheet method in which a team lists what could go wrong at each step of a process, rates each failure and acts on the worst first, to the pipeline that produces a machine-learning model rather than to the model alone. The team works through the pipeline one step at a time (in the 2025 reference version: collect data requests, collect data, ingest data, validate data, preprocess data, train, tune, analyse, deploy and validate the model, and analyse feedback from the field) and, prompted by guide words such as missing, incorrect or too late, records for each step how the resulting model could fail, the effect on the wider system, the pipeline causes, and the current practices that would prevent or catch the failure. Each row is rated for severity, occurrence and detection, and the product of the three, the risk priority number, ranks the rows so that recommended actions and owners go to the highest risks first; severity is taken from the system-level hazard analysis, because the harm a model failure can do depends on the system it sits in. The method's authors publish a pre-populated template listing typical failure modes, causes and mitigations for each step, which a team tailors to its own model and application. The result is a worksheet of ranked pipeline failure modes, their controls and assigned actions, kept up to date as the pipeline changes; it looks at failures one at a time in how the model is built and does not by itself analyse how the deployed system behaves.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous-trucking company's perception team fills in the template for its lane-detection model before each major retraining. One row under 'collect data' records that data gathered in a single season could leave the model unable to see faded or snow-covered markings; its severity comes from the vehicle-level hazard analysis, and it leads to an action, with an owner and a date, to constrain data requests by season and weather before release.

A medical-imaging company preparing a chest X-ray triage model for regulatory review uses the worksheet to show its assessors where the pipeline's controls sit. High-ranked rows include training labels taken from a single radiologist's reading, which could teach the model to miss small nodules, mitigated by double reading of a labelled sample, and online learning in deployment, mitigated by switching it off.

After a warehouse robot's object detector starts misclassifying a new kind of shrink-wrapped pallet, the vendor's safety engineer returns to the worksheet, finds that the 'analyse model feedback' step had no control for new packaging reaching customer sites, adds drift monitoring and a trigger for new data requests, and re-rates the affected rows.

limitations.description: It considers one failure mode at a time, step by step, so it does not show how failures in different steps combine, or how a model that meets its specification can still contribute to an accident through its interaction with people and other parts of the system. Teams that need those combinations and interactions have to pair it with a system-level analysis.

Severity, occurrence and detection are judgements on ordinal scales, and there is little data on how often an ML pipeline failure occurs or how reliably a control catches it. The method's authors introduced ML-specific rating criteria in 2026 because traditional FMEA criteria proved ambiguous for ML development; the public template, last updated in April 2025, has no rating criteria, so teams must set and record their own.

It analyses how the model is built, not how it behaves in use: a complete worksheet shows that known pipeline failure modes have controls, not that the deployed model performs safely. Severity has to come from a system-level hazard analysis, so the method cannot stand alone, and its authors present it as one part of a safety management system and safety case.

The pre-populated template makes a quick start but invites teams to tick through the listed failure modes instead of looking for ones specific to their system. Its examples come mostly from autonomous-vehicle development, so teams in other domains, or with other kinds of model such as language models, must add their own failure modes; the 2026 revision added steps for problem definition and for building ground truth or reward signals.

Published evidence that the method finds failures other methods miss is limited. The 2025 paper that introduced it gave no applied example, and the 2026 follow-up reporting applications to autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots is led by the method's originators: four of its twelve authors, including the first author, wrote the 2025 paper, so no independent group has yet reported using it.

techniques.name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
techniques.description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

resources.title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions
resources.abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

techniques.name: Signal Temporal Logic Monitoring
techniques.description: Signal temporal logic (STL) monitoring checks the signals a system produces over time, such as speeds, distances, positions or a model's outputs, against safety requirements written in signal temporal logic, a formal language for stating how real-valued signals must behave over time intervals (for example, 'whenever the gap to the vehicle ahead falls below 10 m, speed drops below 5 m/s within 2 s'). Each requirement is built from comparisons of signals with thresholds, joined by logical operators and by timed operators such as 'always within [a, b]', 'eventually within [a, b]' and 'until'. For each trace the monitor computes a robustness value, a margin to the requirement rather than robustness to adversarial inputs: its sign says whether the requirement is met (positive) or violated (negative), and its size is a tolerance: any signal whose values stay closer than that to the observed ones at every instant gets the same verdict. Monitors run offline on logged or simulated traces, or online on live signals, where a requirement that looks ahead in time can be decided only once enough of the signal has arrived. RTAMT, the named tool, is an open-source Python library with an optional C++ back-end that builds such monitors from a written specification and connects to ROS and MATLAB/Simulink; its online monitors accept only requirements whose future time windows are bounded and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's time horizon, and it reports the robustness value but does not act on it, so stopping or correcting the system is left to a separate safeguard.

example_use_cases.description: A team developing an adaptive cruise controller with a learned speed policy writes its requirements in STL, for example that the time gap to the vehicle ahead never stays below one second for longer than two seconds, and attaches an RTAMT monitor to every drive in an urban driving simulator. The robustness values show which controller settings meet each requirement and by what margin, and drives with negative values become regression scenarios.

A hospital's service robot, which uses learned perception to find people, fetches supplies along corridors. The integrator monitors live ROS topics against a system requirement (always at least 0.5 m from any detected person) and against one requirement per subsystem, such as the planner reaching its next waypoint in time. When a subsystem requirement fails shortly before the system one, the logged verdicts show where the fault began.

A drone-delivery operator checks each day's flight logs from its learned landing controller against a requirement that, in the last ten seconds before touchdown, descent rate stays below 1 m/s and the drone stays within 0.5 m of the pad centre. It reports the smallest robustness value across all landings to its safety manager and investigates any landing whose value is negative.

limitations.description: The monitor checks the requirement as written, not as intended. Writing correct STL needs fluency in the logic and in the system: a wrong threshold, a time window that is too short or a misplaced operator yields confident positive margins for behaviour the engineers would call unsafe, and nothing in the monitor reveals the mistake. Specifications need the same review as the requirements they encode.

Online monitoring judges a requirement from a partial trace. RTAMT's online monitors take only requirements whose future time windows are bounded, and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's horizon: a check that something happens within five seconds is decided five seconds later, which may be too late to act on in a fast system. Monitors that track a narrowing range of possible robustness values can flag some violations sooner, but stay undecided until the data settles it.

A robustness value is measured in the units of the signals in the requirement, so a margin of 0.4 means 0.4 metres in one requirement and 0.4 degrees in another. Values cannot be compared across requirements, and when one requirement combines signals of different scales its value is set by whichever margin is numerically smallest, which depends on the units chosen unless the signals are normalised first.

Monitoring reports on the traces it sees. A clean record over many hours shows that those runs met the requirement, not that every possible run will, and a violation is reported when it happens, not before, unless a separate predictor of future signals is added. To protect the system, the verdict has to drive a safeguard such as a fallback controller, which the monitor does not provide.

The verdict is only as good as the signals. If a learned perception component misjudges the distance to a person, the monitor computes a confident margin from the wrong distance; independent sensors or ground truth are needed to check the perception itself. Discrete-time monitors see only the samples taken, so a brief violation between samples can go unseen, and the ROS integration assumes messages arrive at a known, regular rate.

techniques.name: SMT-Based Neural Network Verification
techniques.description: SMT-based neural network verification decides exactly whether any input in a defined region can make a trained neural network violate a stated property, and if one can, returns that input as a counterexample. SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers decide whether a set of logical and arithmetic constraints can all hold at once: here the network's weighted sums become linear equations, each piecewise-linear activation such as ReLU becomes a constraint with two cases (inactive at zero, or active and passing its input through), and the input region and the negation of the property become further linear constraints. The solver searches for values that satisfy every constraint with a simplex-based linear-programming engine: it first tries to repair an activation whose current values break it, and splits it into its two cases only when repairs keep failing, while bounds on each neuron (in Marabou, by default, the linear bounds that bound propagation computes) rule cases out early. Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) introduced this lazy treatment of ReLU inside the simplex method and used it on a prototype airborne collision avoidance network; Marabou, its maintained successor, keeps the same search structure with a newer search procedure, adds parallel solving, and can emit a proof certificate for an 'unsatisfiable' answer. The answer is 'unsat', meaning no input in the region violates the property, or 'sat' with a concrete counterexample, and for networks whose activations are all piecewise-linear the procedure is complete; the price is that the number of cases can grow exponentially with the number of neurons, so it is practical for small networks such as controllers, policies and surrogate models with few inputs rather than large image models.

example_use_cases.description: A warehouse robotics team trains hundreds of candidate deep reinforcement learning policies for driving between shelves from range-sensor readings. Before field trials it encodes 'no move into an obstacle in the next step' and 'no repeating left-right loop over several steps' as queries over each small policy network, runs Marabou on every candidate, discards each policy for which a counterexample reading is returned, and takes only the survivors to the physical robot.

An aircraft systems developer replaces a large collision-avoidance lookup table with a set of small neural networks. For each network it writes regions of encounter geometry, such as an intruder close ahead and closing, together with the advisory that must never be issued there, and runs the solver on each. Regions returned as unsatisfiable go into the certification evidence; any counterexample encounter is replayed in simulation and drives retraining.

A medical-device manufacturer uses a small network to recommend infusion rates from a handful of patient measurements. Its safety engineers prove that, for every combination of measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the recommended rate never exceeds the maximum set by the device's hazard analysis, and use any counterexample returned to retrain the network or add an output limit.

limitations.description: Deciding these queries for ReLU networks is NP-complete, and the search may split on every neuron whose case is undecided, so time can grow exponentially with network size and with the number of steps a property spans. In a study of robot navigation policies kept to 16 neurons per hidden layer, single-step collision queries took seconds, but 12-step cycle queries usually ran for hours and nearly three in ten of them hit the 12-hour limit.

The solver runs on ordinary processors, and its own tool paper reports a non-trivial performance gap to GPU-based bound-propagation verifiers, especially on larger networks; in the 2023 verification competition it solved 594 benchmark instances to alpha-beta-CROWN's 721. It is therefore best suited to small networks with few inputs, such as controllers, policies and surrogate models.

Exact answers hold only for piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, max, absolute value and leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh are handled by an over-approximation that is refined step by step, and softmax and bilinear layers only through a convex relaxation, so for networks that use them the procedure is no longer complete and can end without a decisive answer.

The query covers the network and a region of its inputs written as linear constraints, nothing more. A counterexample may lie in a part of the region no real sensor could produce, and a proof says nothing about the environment the network acts in, so choosing a region that is realistic yet small enough to solve takes domain knowledge, and a closed-loop safety claim needs further analysis.

An 'unsat' answer is only as trustworthy as the solver's implementation. Marabou can emit a proof certificate that an independent checker validates, but proof production works with only some of its features and not in parallel mode, and in the tool paper's collision-avoidance experiments certificates were produced for 113 of 180 benchmarks.
