techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Data Validation Checks
techniques.description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider feeds surveillance track reports into a model that predicts aircraft arrival times. Its data engineers run an expectation suite on every incoming batch, covering required fields, units, plausible ranges for altitude and ground speed, and the share of reports with missing positions, so that a sensor change that silently switched altitude from feet to metres would stop the batch before it reached the model rather than surface weeks later as worse predictions.

A weather service that retrains a statistical correction model each month on station observations validates every monthly extract first: station identifiers must come from the station list, temperatures must lie within each station's climatological limits, no variable may have more than 2 per cent missing values, and each variable's mean and quantiles must stay within bounds set from earlier years. A failed check stops the retraining and opens a ticket listing the failing stations.

A hospital running a deterioration-risk model on laboratory results checks each hourly batch from the laboratory system against expectations for test codes, units and value ranges, so that if a laboratory changes the unit of a test without notice the batch is flagged and risk scores for the affected patients are withheld until the mapping is corrected.

A bank's credit-scoring team runs the expectation suite written for its training data on a daily sample of the applications its deployed model scores and compares the results, so that a field the online form has stopped collecting, which the scoring service quietly fills with a default value, shows up as a difference between training and production data rather than as an unexplained drop in approval rates.

limitations.description: Checks catch only what someone thought to write down. A batch can satisfy every rule and still be wrong in a way no rule covers, such as a changed relationship between two columns or a change in how labels were assigned. GX Core does not infer rules from the data, since its automatic profilers were removed in version 1.0, so each rule has to be specified, and for pipelines with thousands of features that effort can put teams off setting up validation at all.

Bounds for distribution rules are hard to set. Statistical tests on large batches fire on differences too small to matter: in Google's data validation paper, a chi-square test between 100 million points and a copy with 0.01 per cent of them redrawn from a wider distribution raised an alert in 7 of 10 trials, while thresholds on divergence measures such as KL divergence are hard for teams to interpret. Bounds are therefore tuned by trial, risking too many alerts or missed shifts.

The rules describe the input data, not the model's performance. A batch that passes can still produce wrong predictions if the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed (concept drift), and a batch that fails shows that the data changed, not that predictions got worse, so the checks need pairing with monitoring of performance once outcomes arrive.

Alerts help only if someone acts on them, and rules need upkeep as data legitimately change. In Google's deployment across more than 700 pipelines, new columns, unexpected values and missing columns were the commonest anomalies, most pipelines revised their schema, and between 28 and 100 per cent of fired anomalies of each kind were fixed, which the authors attribute partly to operators missing or ignoring alerts.

The checks work on tables: GX Core connects to data frames, SQL databases and data files, so for images, audio, free text or gridded weather fields the team must first compute a table of properties, such as sizes, value ranges or missing tiles, and write rules about those. This catches broken or truncated inputs but not changes in what the content shows.

techniques.name: Metamorphic Testing
techniques.description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. Prompt robustness testing and causal discrimination testing in this catalogue each apply one family of invariance relations (meaning-preserving changes to a prompt, and a change of protected attribute), and prompt robustness testing also scores the answers against known ones; metamorphic testing is the general procedure for writing and checking any such relation, including relations that say how the output should change, and needs no known answers.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider evaluating a machine-learning conflict-detection aid for en-route controllers has no ground truth for most replayed traffic samples. Its test team writes three relations: swapping two aircraft's call signs, shifting every timestamp by the same amount, and rotating the whole sample together with its wind field must not change which aircraft pairs are flagged. It runs them on a year of recorded traffic and holds the release until every violation is explained.

A supplier of lidar obstacle perception for driverless shuttles cannot label every frame it records. Following a relation implied by the perception specification, its test team adds a few hundred random points outside the mapped road area to recorded frames and checks that no obstacle detected in the original frame disappears, reporting the share of frames where one does, by number of points added, as a release criterion for each software build.

A weather service testing a neural network that nowcasts rainfall from radar images checks a relation expected from the way rain moves with the wind: away from the domain's edges, shifting the input radar sequence a few grid cells east should shift the forecast rain field by the same amount, within a tolerance set from the model's day-to-day error. Forecasters review the breaking cases to judge whether the model has learnt a dependence on location, such as on terrain, that it should keep.

A bank moving its credit-scoring models to a new library cannot treat every difference from the old library's outputs as a fault, since the solvers differ. Its validation team writes relations the mathematics guarantees: reordering the input columns, or adding a constant to a numeric input in training and scoring data of a logistic regression with an unpenalised intercept, must leave every predicted probability unchanged within solver tolerance. Each violation is investigated as a fault.

limitations.description: Passing shows that outputs are consistent, not that they are correct. A model that gives the same wrong answer for a source case and its follow-up satisfies the relation, and one that is wrong in the same way everywhere can pass every invariance relation. On its own the technique therefore does not suit systems where each output must be shown to be right, and it complements rather than replaces testing against known answers where those exist.

The evidence is only as good as the relations, which are written by hand from domain knowledge, with no systematic way to choose among the many possible ones. A relation the system is not bound to obey produces false alarms: in a study of the Weka library, violations by its nearest-neighbour classifier came from legitimate tie-breaking between equally likely labels, not from faults. An incomplete set of relations gives false confidence.

Most model outputs need a tolerance, and the result depends heavily on it. In the DeepTest study of three driving models, violations under simple image transformations fell from 23,391 when a transformed frame's squared error against the human steering label could be at most the original mean squared error to 330 when it could be five times that, and manual review still found false positives. Counts compare only between runs with the same tolerance, set from what the application can accept.

Follow-up inputs are synthetic and may not occur in practice: rain or fog added to an image, or points scattered into a lidar frame, approximate real conditions without reproducing them. A violation on an unrealistic input may not matter in operation, and a pass covers only the transformations tried, so the evidence is about the tested relations and transformations, not the operating conditions as a whole.

A model whose outputs vary between runs on the same input, through sampling, seeds or GPU arithmetic, breaks relations by chance, so runs must be made repeatable or each case repeated and judged statistically. This bites hardest for relations over the training data, such as Xie et al.'s for classifiers, which need the model retrained for every follow-up case; for models that are costly to train only prediction-time relations are practical, and they test the trained model, not its training.

resources.title: Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases
resources.abstract: In software testing, a set of test cases is constructed according to some predefined selection criteria. The software is then examined against these test cases. Three interesting observations have been made on the current artifacts of software testing. Firstly, an error-revealing test case is considered useful while a successful test case which does not reveal software errors is usually not further investigated. Whether these successful test cases still contain useful information for revealing software errors has not been properly studied. Secondly, no matter how extensive the testing has been conducted in the development phase, errors may still exist in the software [5]. These errors, if left undetected, may eventually cause damage to the production system. The study of techniques for uncovering software errors in the production phase is seldom addressed in the literature. Thirdly, as indicated by Weyuker in [6], the availability of test oracles is pragmatically unattainable in most situations. However, the availability of test oracles is generally assumed in conventional software testing techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel test case selection technique that derives new test cases from the successful ones. The selection aims at revealing software errors that are possibly left undetected in successful test cases which may be generated using some existing strategies. As such, the proposed technique augments the effectiveness of existing test selection strategies. The technique also helps uncover software errors in the production phase and can be used in the absence of test oracles.

techniques.name: Reliability Diagram with Expected Calibration Error
techniques.description: A reliability diagram with expected calibration error (ECE) measures whether a classifier's stated confidence matches how often it is right, so that a reader can tell whether predictions given a probability of 70 per cent come true about 70 per cent of the time. Using labelled cases the model was not trained on, each prediction's confidence (the probability given to the predicted class, or to an event such as rain above a threshold) is placed in one of a fixed number of bins, commonly ten or fifteen equal-width intervals between 0 and 1, and in each bin the average confidence is compared with the observed frequency, the share of its cases in which the predicted class or event actually occurred. The reliability diagram plots observed frequency against average confidence bin by bin, so that bins below the diagonal show overconfidence and bins above it underconfidence, and is usually shown with a histogram of how many cases fall in each bin, which the diagram itself does not show; the ECE condenses the same comparison into one number, the average gap between confidence and observed frequency weighted by each bin's share of the cases, and the maximum calibration error reports the largest gap in any bin. The technique measures and changes nothing: Platt scaling, isotonic regression calibration and temperature scaling repair a model's probabilities, and this measurement, run before and after on the same held-out cases, none of them used to fit the repair, is the evidence that a repair worked.

example_use_cases.description: A national meteorological service is deciding whether to issue a neural-network nowcast's probabilities that radar reflectivity will exceed set thresholds within the next hour. On a held-out season of radar composites, its verification team draws reliability diagrams with sample-count histograms and computes the ECE for each threshold and lead time beside those of its current extrapolation ensemble, and issues the new probabilities only for thresholds where they are at least as reliable.

A hospital's imaging AI group receives a chest X-ray classifier whose vendor reports good calibration on public data. Before connecting it, the group computes the reliability diagram and ECE on a year of its own labelled studies, finds the model overconfident in its highest bins, fits temperature scaling on a separate validation split, and repeats the measurement on the untouched test split to show whether the gap has closed.

A law firm's knowledge team evaluating a language-model research assistant that reports a confidence with each answer asks it a held-out set of questions with verified answers, bins its self-reported confidence, and computes the reliability diagram and ECE for each practice area rather than only for the whole set. The confidence display is switched off for practice areas where the gap between stated confidence and accuracy exceeds the firm's threshold.

A card issuer's fraud team checks its transaction-risk model each month on transactions whose outcomes have arrived, using bins fixed at validation that are narrow over the high scores where alerts are raised. Because fraud is rare, nearly all cases fall in the lowest bin and dominate the ECE, so the team tracks the gap in each high-score bin as well; a gap above the limit set at model sign-off triggers an investigation of drift and a decision on recalibration.

limitations.description: The result depends on how predictions are binned. With equal-width bins, confident models put most cases in one or two bins, which dominate the ECE while the others rest on few cases; more bins give a finer measurement but a noisier estimate in each bin. Rankings of recalibration methods can change with the number of bins or the binning scheme, so both must be reported and held fixed in any comparison.

Binning distorts the estimate in both directions. Overconfident and underconfident predictions in the same bin cancel, so with plenty of data the binned ECE understates the true error. On small samples, sampling noise inflates it: with 15 equal-width bins, a simulated perfectly calibrated model showed large errors on 200 cases. ECEs from samples of different sizes, such as subgroups, are not directly comparable; equal-mass bins or a debiased estimator reduce the bias.

Calibration says nothing about how well the model separates cases. A model that gives every case the overall base rate, such as 0.5 on a balanced dataset, is calibrated but useless, so the ECE must be reported with accuracy, the area under the ROC curve or a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score, which combines calibration with how decisive the predictions are.

Weighting by bin size gives rare but important predictions almost no weight. In a precipitation nowcasting study, almost all probabilities for heavy-rain thresholds fell in the lowest bin, so the ECE barely registered the rare high-probability forecasts, and at the highest threshold it could not be compared because some bins were empty. For multi-class models the usual ECE also looks only at the top predicted class and ignores the calibration of the others.

The measurement holds only for the population and period it was computed on. One ECE over a whole test set can hide large differences between subgroups: in an evaluation of language models answering medical questions, ECE ranged from 0.041 to 0.141 across specialties, a spread the pooled figure masked. Calibration can also drift after deployment, so it has to be measured for the subgroups that matter and repeated on new labelled data.

resources.title: Obtaining Well Calibrated Probabilities Using Bayesian Binning
On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

In every month of 2026, in each high-score bin fixed at model sign-off, the fraud model's average predicted probability was within two percentage points of the observed fraud rate among transactions with confirmed outcomes.

techniques.name: Continuous Ranked Probability Score
techniques.description: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast of a numerical quantity, such as tomorrow's temperature or next week's demand, by scoring the whole predicted distribution, not just a single best guess, against the value later observed. For each case it compares the forecast's cumulative distribution (the predicted probability that the outcome will fall below each possible value) with a step that jumps from 0 to 1 at the observed value, squares the gap at every value and adds these up, which is the same as adding up the Brier score of the yes-or-no forecasts 'the outcome will be below this value' over every possible threshold. For a forecast given as an ensemble or a sample it can be computed as the average distance between the members and the observation minus half the average distance between pairs of members, closed forms exist for common distributions such as the Gaussian, and for a single-value forecast it reduces to the absolute error, so probabilistic and deterministic forecasts can be compared directly. The score is proper: a forecaster expects the best score by reporting the distribution they actually believe, so it cannot be improved on average by making forecasts narrower or wider than warranted, and it is lowest when the forecast distribution matches how outcomes actually vary. Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

example_use_cases.description: A national weather service deciding whether to run a machine-learning ensemble alongside its physics-based ensemble scores both against a year of station observations, computing the fair CRPS (the two ensembles differ in size) for 2-metre temperature and 10-metre wind at every station and lead time. It adopts the new system only for the variables and lead times where its CRPS skill relative to the existing ensemble is positive.

A wind-farm operator choosing between two vendors of probabilistic power forecasts for day-ahead trading receives 19 quantiles per hour from each. It approximates each forecast's CRPS by averaging the quantile scores across those levels and compares the vendors over a full winter against metered output. Because high-output hours drive balancing costs, it also compares them on a version of the score weighted towards the upper quantiles, averaged over all hours, not only those with high output.

A hospital group's capacity team plans elective admissions with a probabilistic forecast of bed occupancy one week ahead. Each week it computes the forecast's CRPS against the occupancy that followed and its skill score against a seasonal naive forecast, and a rolling eight-week skill score below zero triggers a review of the model before it is used for the next planning cycle.

limitations.description: One CRPS value combines calibration (whether outcomes behave like draws from the forecast distribution) and sharpness (how narrow the forecast is), so a better score does not show which improved, and an average over many cases can hide conditions in which forecasts are consistently too narrow or too wide. A claim about calibration needs Hersbach's decomposition of the score into reliability and resolution parts, a rank histogram or a spread-skill check as well.

Every threshold carries equal weight and extreme outcomes are rare, so the average score says little about how well extremes are forecast; WeatherBench 2 notes that the CRPS does not specifically focus on extreme weather. Averaging only over cases in which an extreme occurred does not repair this and can discredit skilful forecasters (Lerch et al. 2017); claims about warnings of extremes need a threshold-weighted CRPS that emphasises the tails.

It scores one quantity at one place and lead time at a time, so it does not test whether a forecast gets the relationships between places, times or variables right. WeatherBench 2 notes that its CRPS results ignore spatial and temporal correlation, and found models trained on each wind component separately biased in wind speed; claims about joint quantities, such as rainfall totalled over a catchment, need a multivariate score such as the energy score.

The score is in the units of the forecast quantity and grows with how variable that quantity is, so raw values cannot be compared or pooled across variables, locations or seasons with different variability, and averages are dominated by the most variable cases. Comparisons across these need a skill score relative to a stated reference forecast, and the choice of reference, such as climatology or persistence, changes the result.

For an ensemble, the usual estimate treats the members as the whole forecast distribution, which penalises small ensembles: if two systems draw members from the same distribution, the one with fewer members scores worse on average. Ferro (2014) showed the usual ensemble CRPS is unfair in this sense and gave an adjusted fair version, which libraries such as scoringrules provide; it should be used whenever ensembles of different sizes are compared.

techniques.name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
techniques.description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.

techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.

techniques.name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
techniques.description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's cardiology informatics team has a deep network that measures intervals and amplitudes from 12-lead ECGs and must choose which heatmap method to show cardiologists. It perturbs the highest-ranked sample points first, one per step, tracks the rise in measurement error over several thousand ECGs, and compares each method's area under the error curve with that of random heatmaps. Because expert preferences and the curves can disagree, it reports both before choosing.

A regulator's data team routes consumer complaints with a fine-tuned transformer classifier and wants to highlight for caseworkers the words behind each routing decision. Before choosing between two word-attribution methods, it computes comprehensiveness and sufficiency on a validation sample at the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs and adopts a method only if it clearly beats randomly ranked words on both measures.

A rail operator's engineering team uses an image classifier to flag defects in track inspection photographs and wants heatmaps that point inspectors to the defect. It runs deletion with pixels set to a constant and insertion from a blurred image for three heatmap methods, then repeats the deletion run with a second replacement value, and adopts a method only if it ranks first under both.

limitations.description: Removing pixels or words produces inputs unlike anything the model was trained on, so part of the drop in score can be the model reacting to an unfamiliar input rather than to the loss of the information the explanation pointed to, and the shape of the removed region can itself carry class information. Results are least trustworthy when large parts of the input are removed; variants that retrain the model or fill removed pixels from their neighbours reduce the effect.

The score depends on how features are removed and in what order. On one image classifier, the best-ranked method changed when removed pixels were set to the dataset mean instead of random colours, removing the least relevant pixels first ranked the methods roughly in reverse of removing the most relevant first, and rankings varied from image to image. A comparison holds only for the stated replacement value, order, step size and fraction removed, and should be checked under a second replacement.

Only the order of the attribution scores counts, not their size, so explanations with very different magnitudes can receive the same score. Taking absolute values of signed attributions changes the order and hence the result. The curves cannot tell an explanation that ranks the right features but gives them misleading magnitudes from one that gets both right; that needs a measure that uses the attribution values.

The curves show whether the ranking tracks the model, not whether the explanation is useful or correct for the domain: a model that relies on a spurious cue receives a faithful explanation of that cue. In a study of ECG models, ECG experts' choice of the best heatmap method disagreed considerably with the perturbation ranking, so a good curve does not show that experts will find the explanation helpful.

Each curve needs one model evaluation per step, for every input and method compared, so fine-grained curves over large images, long documents or big test sets are expensive. In the original region-perturbation study, two settings over 5,040 images each, with 100 steps repeated ten times because the replacement values were random, took roughly 36 hours on a workstation with 20 hyper-threaded Xeon cores in 2015. Coarser steps cut the cost but make the curve less able to separate methods.

techniques.name: Explanation Infidelity
techniques.description: Explanation infidelity scores a feature-attribution explanation (one importance score per input feature) by how well it predicts what the model does when the input is changed. The evaluator chooses a distribution of meaningful perturbations, for example small random noise around a reference input, or setting random subsets of features or square patches of an image to a reference value, and draws many perturbations from it. For each one it compares the change in output that the explanation predicts, the sum over features of each feature's perturbation multiplied by its attribution score, with the change the model actually shows, its output on the original input minus its output on the perturbed one. Infidelity is the average squared difference between the two, estimated by random sampling, so lower is better; Yeh et al. (2019), who proposed it, showed that several common explanation methods each have the lowest infidelity for one particular perturbation distribution, so the distribution chosen defines what counts as faithful in a given test. Scores are averaged over a set of inputs and compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, under the same perturbations; unlike a deletion curve, the score uses the size of each attribution as well as its rank.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team must choose which attribution method supplies the reason scores shown to credit analysts for a neural-network default model. It computes infidelity on held-out applications for three candidate methods, with perturbations that set random subsets of features to a documented reference applicant and with rescaling switched on, and records the perturbation distribution in the validation report beside the method it selects.

A manufacturer's quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defects in weld radiographs and smooths its gradient heatmaps by averaging them over noisy copies of each image. It sets the amount of noise by computing infidelity under square-patch perturbations sized to typical defects on validation radiographs and choosing the level with the lowest score, since in the original study infidelity first fell and then rose as smoothing increased.

A hospital's clinical AI team retrains its deterioration-risk model each quarter and shows ward staff the attribution scores behind each alert. After every retraining it recomputes rescaled infidelity on the latest validation data, with the perturbations fixed at first validation, for the deployed attribution settings and two alternatives, and holds the release for review if the deployed settings are no longer the lowest, since the absolute score also moves with the retrained model.

limitations.description: What counts as faithful is set by the perturbation distribution. Yeh et al. show that several common explanations each have the lowest possible infidelity for one particular distribution (for example, Shapley values for the feature-subset scheme that SHAP uses), so a comparison can be won by choosing matching perturbations. The distribution should be fixed in advance and justified by the question the explanation is meant to answer.

The score is a squared error between predicted and actual changes in output, so it depends on the scale of the attribution scores: two methods that rank features identically but on different scales get different infidelity. Yeh et al. rescale each explanation optimally before scoring, and Captum offers this rescaling as an option that is off by default; without it, comparisons across methods mislead.

Some attribution methods multiply each feature's sensitivity by the input's distance from a reference and others do not, and the perturbation term has to be computed to match. Yeh et al. compare the two kinds separately, and Captum asks the user to state which kind is being scored; getting this wrong produces a score that reflects the mismatch rather than the explanation.

It follows from the definition, though Yeh et al. do not discuss it, that the predicted change is a sum of per-feature effects. Where the model's response to the chosen perturbations is not additive, as when pixels within an object or words within a phrase interact, no attribution can reach zero infidelity. The floor is the same for every method scored on the same model and perturbations, so rankings stand, but the score is not the explanation's error alone and cannot be compared across models.

The score is an average over random perturbations, each needing a model evaluation. Yeh et al. used 1,000 perturbations per input; Captum's default is 10. Few samples give noisy scores, so small differences between methods need repeated runs, while many samples multiply the cost by the inputs, methods and settings compared. Quantus's built-in version perturbs square patches and so handles image data only.

resources.title: On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity of Explanations
resources.abstract: We consider objective evaluation measures of saliency explanations for complex black-box machine learning models. We propose simple robust variants of two notions that have been considered in recent literature: (in)fidelity, and sensitivity. We analyze optimal explanations with respect to both these measures, and while the optimal explanation for sensitivity is a vacuous constant explanation, the optimal explanation for infidelity is a novel combination of two popular explanation methods. By varying the perturbation distribution that defines infidelity, we obtain novel explanations by optimizing infidelity, which we show to out-perform existing explanations in both quantitative and qualitative measurements. Another salient question given these measures is how to modify any given explanation to have better values with respect to these measures. We propose a simple modification based on lowering sensitivity, and moreover show that when done appropriately, we could simultaneously improve both sensitivity as well as fidelity.

techniques.name: Explanation Max-Sensitivity
techniques.description: Explanation max-sensitivity measures how stable an explanation is: whether inputs that differ only slightly, in ways that should not change the answer, receive very different explanations. For each input, the evaluator samples many nearby points within a small radius (for example, no feature moved by more than 0.02 on a 0 to 1 scale), recomputes the explanation at each with the same explanation method, and records the largest distance between a recomputed explanation and the original; Yeh et al. (2019) defined the measure and estimated it by random sampling. Dividing each change in the explanation by the distance the input moved, and taking the largest ratio, gives the closely related local Lipschitz estimate of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), which they maximised with an optimiser rather than by sampling; the two are not interchangeable, because the ratio is dominated by the smallest input changes and can be unbounded where max-sensitivity is finite, so they can rank methods differently. Lower scores mean a more stable explanation, and scores are compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, on the same inputs, radius and distance measure. The test treats the explanation method as a black box, so it applies to attribution scores from any method, but on its own it says nothing about faithfulness: a constant explanation that ignores the model is perfectly stable.

example_use_cases.description: A consumer lender tells declined applicants the main reasons for each decision, taken from Shapley-value attributions of its credit model. Its model-risk team measures max-sensitivity on a sample of declined applications, perturbing features only within bounds the lending policy treats as immaterial, to choose between two sampling budgets for the explainer, because applicants who differ trivially should not be given different main reasons.

An Earth-observation team comparing attribution methods for a multi-label land-cover classifier on satellite image patches computes max-sensitivity for each method together with a most-relevant-first deletion curve, and short-lists methods that do well on both. Pairing the two matters because smoothing an explanation lowers its sensitivity, and a stable method is worth choosing only if it also tracks the model.

A vehicle perception team averages gradient heatmaps over noisy copies of each camera frame to steady them for safety reviewers. It sets the noise level by tracking max-sensitivity and infidelity together on validation frames as the level rises, and picks the point where sensitivity has levelled off before infidelity starts to increase, since too much smoothing produces stable maps that no longer reflect the detector.

limitations.description: A low score does not mean the explanation is right. The most stable explanation possible is a constant one that ignores the model, and heavy smoothing keeps lowering sensitivity while eventually making the explanation less faithful. Max-sensitivity should be reported with a measure of faithfulness on the same inputs, and a method should not be chosen for stability alone.

The sampled maximum is a lower bound on the true worst case: with a handful of random samples per input (Captum's default is 10), the largest change found can be far below the largest that exists. Deliberately chosen perturbations that leave the prediction unchanged can alter explanations dramatically, so a low score does not show that explanations resist manipulation.

The number depends on settings that differ between tools: the radius, the distance measure for inputs and explanations, the number of samples and whether explanations are normalised first. By default Captum samples 10 points within a radius of 0.02 and Quantus 200 points within 0.2, ten times wider, while Yeh et al. used 50 points within 0.1 and normalised explanations to unit length. Scores are comparable only under identical settings and identically scaled inputs.

A high score can come from the model rather than the explanation method. Near a decision boundary, or where the model's output changes quickly, a faithful explanation should change, and Yeh et al. note that explanations built from the model's own sensitivity can be more sensitive than the model. Perturbations that change the prediction should be excluded or reported separately.

The test assumes inputs can be nudged by small continuous amounts. For words, categories or other discrete inputs no such small change exists, and the fallback of comparing explanations of similar examples already in the test data is weaker and depends on how many close neighbours the data contain. The per-unit Lipschitz form can be unbounded for gradient explanations of ReLU networks, one reason Yeh et al. prefer the undivided maximum, which stays finite.

resources.title: On the Robustness of Interpretability Methods
resources.abstract: We argue that robustness of explanations---i.e., that similar inputs should give rise to similar explanations---is a key desideratum for interpretability. We introduce metrics to quantify robustness and demonstrate that current methods do not perform well according to these metrics. Finally, we propose ways that robustness can be enforced on existing interpretability approaches.

techniques.name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
techniques.description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.abstract:
Saliency methods have emerged as a popular tool to highlight features in an input
deemed relevant for the prediction of a learned model. Several saliency methods
have been proposed, often guided by visual appeal on image data. In this work, we
propose an actionable methodology to evaluate what kinds of explanations a given
method can and cannot provide. We find that reliance, solely, on visual assessment
can be misleading. Through extensive experiments we show that some existing
saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating
process. Consequently, methods that fail the proposed tests are inadequate for
tasks that are sensitive to either data or model, such as, finding outliers in the data,
explaining the relationship between inputs and outputs that the model learned,
and debugging the model. We interpret our findings through an analogy with
edge detection in images, a technique that requires neither training data nor model.
Theory in the case of a linear model and a single-layer convolutional neural network
supports our experimental findings.

Assessing the Trustworthiness of Saliency Maps for Localizing                     Abnormalities in Medical Imaging
Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

sample_claims.text: Every saliency method used in the chest-radiograph review tool produced maps whose structural similarity to the original fell below the agreed threshold once the top blocks of the network were randomised, on a held-out sample of radiographs.

For the fraud model's attribution scores, rank correlation without absolute values between original and layer-randomised attributions is below the threshold set in the validation plan for every layer tested.

Heatmaps from the methods kept for the gearbox dashboard differ between the network trained on true fault labels and the same architecture trained on shuffled labels, by more than the threshold stated in the test report.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.
